query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Thermal aging of as-cast Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys induces a transformation from a metastable microstructure—with fine, dispersed intermetallic compounds in a solid solution matrix—to a more equilibrium state characterized by coarsened and stabilized intermetallic phases. This microstructural evolution improves the continuity and composition of protective passive films, thereby enhancing corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation behavior compared to the as-cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast non-equilibrium Mg-containing high-entropy alloy (density <6 g/cm³) with heterogeneous microstructure comprising solid solutions and fine intermetallic compounds.
generation.intervention: Systematic thermal aging (heat treatment) designed to promote the nucleation, growth, and coarsening of intermetallic phases.
generation.conditions: Controlled comparison between as-cast (baseline) and thermally aged specimens under standardized corrosion conditions (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization in a defined corrosive medium) and high-temperature oxidation testing.
generation.structural_mediator: Transformation and coarsening of intermetallic compounds which modify the passive film formation along with local chemical gradients at phase boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Thermal aging facilitates the nucleation and growth of stable intermetallic phases, reducing microstructural heterogeneities that hinder the formation of a continuous and protective passive film. The re-distribution of elements at phase boundaries during aging alters local corrosion behavior and slows oxidation kinetics by forming a more adherent, compositionally favorable oxide layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast alloy, thermally aged samples will exhibit lower corrosion current densities and reduced high-temperature oxidation rates (e.g., thinner, more adherent oxide scales), evidencing improved performance.
generation.baseline: The as-cast state, which exhibits a metastable microstructure with fine intermetallics leading to less effective passive film formation, higher corrosion current densities, and faster oxidation kinetics.
generation.boundary: The experimental conditions are limited to alloys with density below 6 g/cm³ and within the chemical composition range of Mg-containing high-entropy alloys; performance measurements are taken under standardized corrosion and high-temperature oxidation testing conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvements in corrosion resistance and oxidation kinetics and their sensitivity to specific aging temperatures and durations remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens from the same as-cast alloy batch. Subject one set to a defined thermal aging treatment while retaining the other set as a baseline. Characterize microstructures using SEM/TEM to verify intermetallic coarsening, perform potentiodynamic polarization to assess corrosion behavior, and conduct high-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., using thermogravimetric analysis and oxide scale characterization via XPS) to evaluate oxidation resistance.
measurements: Corrosion current density and potential from polarization tests
Oxide scale thickness, morphology, and adhesion
Passive film composition from surface analyses
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If thermal aging does not result in a significant increase in intermetallic phase coarsening or if the aged samples do not display statistically significant improvements in corrosion resistance (i.e., reduction in corrosion current density) and high-temperature oxidation behavior (i.e., formation of a more adherent or thinner oxide scale) compared to the as-cast baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

decision.trend: Early work on lightweight, Mg-containing high‐ and complex concentrated alloys has emphasized non‐equilibrium processing to achieve metastable microstructures that combine solid solution regions with intermetallic compounds. Researchers initially used induction melting or mechanical alloying (e.g., ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering) to create alloys whose phase stability and hardness were correlated with Mg and other elemental contents. Subsequent studies noted region‐dependent properties—such as differing corrosion resistance in compositionally graded samples—but they did not sufficiently resolve the transformation pathways from metastable states into more equilibrium microstructures. In essence, the progression has been from establishing desirable low-density, high-strength alloys to observing phase evolution with hints that the emergence or growth of stable intermetallic compounds may influence corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior.
decision.unsolved: The unanswered question is the mechanistic link between the evolution (i.e., the transformation from metastable, non-equilibrium microstructures to an equilibrium or quasi-equilibrium state featuring stable intermetallic compounds) and its specific impact on corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation. Notably, it remains unclear whether the transformation—such as the nucleation, growth, or coarsening of intermetallic phases—alters the composition and continuity of passive films or changes the diffusional pathways that govern oxidation kinetics and corrosion behavior.
decision.lever: systematic thermal aging (heat-treatment) applied to a baseline non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy to promote controlled transformation of metastable phases into stable intermetallic compounds, followed by direct comparisons of corrosion (via potentiodynamic polarization in a standardized corrosive medium) and high-temperature oxidation performance
decision.why: This approach naturally extends previous work by using controlled thermal treatments to force the evolution of the microstructure. By comparing an as-cast (metastable) baseline and an identically processed but thermally aged sample, the experiment will test whether the induced transformation—specifically the formation or coarsening of intermetallic phases—directly correlates with measurable changes in passive film formation, corrosion resistance, and oxidation kinetics. A lack of predicted performance enhancement (or a worsening of properties) under the defined boundary conditions would falsify the hypothesis, thereby clarifying the role of metastable-to-equilibrium evolution in these alloys.
